units.sourceHTML: 5.2 Basic (BRE) and extended (ERE) regular expression

units.text: Basic and extended regular expressions are two variations on the syntax of the specified pattern. Basic Regular Expression (BRE) syntax is the default in ⟦0⟧ (and similarly in ⟦1⟧). Use the POSIX-specified ⟦2⟧ option (⟦3⟧, ⟦4⟧) to enable Extended Regular Expression (ERE) syntax.
units.sourceHTML: Basic and extended regular expressions are two variations on the syntax of the specified pattern. Basic Regular Expression (BRE) syntax is the default in sed (and similarly in grep). Use the POSIX-specified -E option (-r, --regexp-extended) to enable Extended Regular Expression (ERE) syntax.

units.text: In GNU ⟦0⟧, the only difference between basic and extended regular expressions is in the behavior of a few special characters: ‘⟦1⟧’, ‘⟦2⟧’, parentheses, braces (‘⟦3⟧’), and ‘⟦4⟧’.
units.sourceHTML: In GNU sed, the only difference between basic and extended regular expressions is in the behavior of a few special characters: ‘?’, ‘+’, parentheses, braces (‘{}’), and ‘|’.

units.text: With basic (BRE) syntax, these characters do not have special meaning unless prefixed with a backslash (‘⟦0⟧’); While with extended (ERE) syntax it is reversed: these characters are special unless they are prefixed with backslash (‘⟦1⟧’).
units.sourceHTML: With basic (BRE) syntax, these characters do not have special meaning unless prefixed with a backslash (‘\’); While with extended (ERE) syntax it is reversed: these characters are special unless they are prefixed with backslash (‘\’).

units.text: One or more ‘⟦0⟧’ characters followed by ‘⟦1⟧’ (plus sign as special meta-character)
units.sourceHTML: One or more ‘a’ characters followed by ‘b’ (plus sign as special meta-character)
